analysis.one_liner: Requires lead-paint testing and safe relocation for young kids in federally assisted housing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past committee: introduced in March 2016 with three Democratic cosponsors, it received no committee action or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the EPA and HUD to update federal standards for lead-contaminated dust and soil to match current health science, defined lead poisoning in children at 5 micrograms per deciliter of blood, and closed a loophole for studio apartments. For families with a child under age 6 moving into federally assisted housing built before 1978, it would have required an actual lead-hazard risk assessment before move-in — a visual check would no longer count — and guaranteed emergency relocation to a lead-safe unit with no waitlist or loss of assistance. It also ordered the Government Accountability Office to report on lead hazards in federally assisted housing and the costs of fixing them.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families with young children living in or moving into federally assisted housing built before 1978, where lead paint hazards are most common. Lead poisoning in young children causes permanent learning and developmental damage, and the bill would have caught hazards before a child moved in rather than after a blood test showed poisoning.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young kids in assisted housing

how_it_helps.text: Requires an initial lead-based paint hazard risk assessment — not just a visual check — before a family with a child under 6 occupies federally assisted housing built before 1978.
Guarantees families with a lead-poisoned child emergency relocation to a lead-free unit, with no waitlist placement, no penalty, and no lapse in housing assistance.
Directs the EPA to update standards for lead-contaminated dust and soil to health-based levels, and directs HUD to match them, closing the gap between old regulations and current science.
Defines an elevated blood lead level at 5 micrograms per deciliter or the latest CDC definition, and removes 0-bedroom (studio) units from the definition of target housing so they cannot be exempted.

Orders the Government Accountability Office to report on lead hazards in federally assisted housing, including whether federal funding meets the need and how remediation requirements would affect landlord participation and the affordable housing stock.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and owners of pre-1978 federally assisted housing, who would bear the cost of risk assessments and hazard remediation before leasing to families with young children, and taxpayers, since the bill authorized appropriations 'as may be necessary' without naming a specific amount.
analysis.who_pays_short: Owners of older assisted rental housing

drawbacks.text: The bill's own GAO-report provision acknowledges the central tradeoff: requiring risk assessments beyond visual checks could raise costs for landlords and reduce landlord participation in federal housing programs, shrinking the stock of affordable housing.

It exempted single-family housing covered by an FHA mortgage-insurance application, and multifamily FHA properties with no other federal assistance, leaving a gap in coverage for some federally financed homes.

It authorized appropriations 'as may be necessary' without specifying funding, so landlords might have faced new unfunded compliance obligations, and Congress would have had to appropriate money separately for abatement to work at scale.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and one-directional: lead exposure causes irreversible brain damage in children, and the bill targeted the exact homes where the government already has leverage — housing it finances or subsidizes. The honest cost is on landlords, and the bill itself directed a GAO study of whether stricter inspections would push landlords out of federal programs and shrink affordable housing supply. Weighing permanent child brain damage against landlord inspection costs, the tradeoff favors the children; the funding vagueness was the bill's weakest design feature.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2016, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2017, so it died without a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on March 3, 2016, with Sen. Menendez, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

Three senators — all Democrats — cosponsored it, and no further action of any kind, including a committee markup, hearing vote, or floor vote, appears in the action history before the 114th Congress ended.

Congress adjourned on January 3, 2017, and the bill was never reintroduced or acted on in that Congress, leaving federal lead-dust and lead-soil standards and pre-occupancy inspection rules unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of pre-1978 federally assisted rental housing, who avoided new testing and remediation obligations, and the status quo in which hazards are often found only after a child is poisoned. Families with young children in assisted housing gained nothing.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no markup, no hearing vote, no report — after referral in March 2016, keeping it off the Senate floor.

against.name: Richard Shelby
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair in the 114th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, so it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so positions are unknown; the only recorded support was from four Democrats, and no Republican publicly opposed or supported the bill in the record.

industries.industry: Landlords and owners of federally assisted pre-1978 housing
industries.note: The bill would have required pre-occupancy lead risk assessments and remediation, or loss of lead-free tenants through guaranteed relocation, at the owner's expense. Its interest in avoiding those costs runs directly against children's health, and the bill died before any of it applied.

Mandatory risk assessments before occupancy and stricter dust and soil standards would have created demand for professional lead inspections and abatement work. In this case the industry's growth depends on doing the safety work families need.

industries.industry: Federal Housing Administration mortgage lending and insured landlords
industries.note: The bill carved single-family FHA-financed homes and multifamily FHA properties without other assistance out of the risk-assessment requirement, so FHA-financed landlords would have avoided the compliance costs their assisted-housing counterparts faced.
